title: Cytoplasmic Phase Sensing: A New Biophysical Concept Linking Environmental Stress Perception to Adaptive Reorganization of the Plant Cell
content: Plant cells are commonly described as sensing environmental stress through specialized molecular receptors that initiate canonical signalling cascades ultimately leading to transcriptional reprogramming. Although this receptor-centred view is strongly supported by experimental evidence, it leaves an explanatory gap: many physiological adjustments to dehydration, heat and cold stress, as well as osmotic imbalance, begin within seconds to minutes—substantially earlier than receptor-initiated transcription could plausibly account for these changes. Over the past decade, studies of biomolecular condensates and liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) have shown that numerous plant and non-plant proteins can change their material state—from freely diffusing monomers to liquid droplets, gels, or glass-like states—directly in response to the same physicochemical variables that stress imposes on the cytoplasm: hydration, ionic strength, pH, redox potential, macromolecular crowding, and temperature. These phenomena are typically considered separately for individual types of condensates, without an explicit conceptual layer linking the physical state of the cytoplasm as a whole to the classical Ca²⁺–ROS–hormone–transcription signalling architecture. In this work, we synthesize existing experimental and theoretical evidence and propose the concept of Cytoplasmic Phase Sensing (CPS), on the basis of which we develop the Cytoplasmic Phase Sensing Theory (CPST). The theory proposes that a living plant cell can convert environmentally induced physicochemical perturbations into regulated changes in cytoplasmic phase organization, molecular mobility, and material state, and that these transitions contribute to shaping subsequent metabolic, hormonal, and transcriptional responses. As the strongest currently available mechanistic example, we consider dehydration, examining established patterns of macromolecular crowding, liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS), stress granules, mechanosensitive channels, Ca²⁺/ROS/ABA/TOR–SnRK1 signalling pathways, and stress memory. We explicitly distinguish experimentally established evidence, mechanistic inferences, and the new hypothesis proposed in this work. We identify what is genuinely novel in this concept relative to existing approaches—including classical homeostasis, proteostasis, receptor-mediated signalling, mechanosensing, and LLPS biology when considered separately—and formulate falsifiable and methodologically testable predictions, complemented by a discussion of the strongest arguments against the proposed concept. Cytoplasmic Phase Sensing is presented not as an established mechanism, but as a structured hypothesis intended to organize future experimental research at the interface of plant stress physiology and cellular biophysics.
